query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium, rapidly solidified Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs), the initially homogeneous metastable solid solution evolves under high-temperature oxidizing conditions by diffusively segregating Mg to grain boundaries and interfaces. This segregation promotes the in situ formation of stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds which act as nucleation sites for a dense, adherent MgO scale. In turn, the formation of this protective oxide layer reduces local corrosion rates and modifies the high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: Rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g., Al–Mg–Cu–Zn–Gd) with a predominantly metastable solid solution matrix containing dispersed, less developed intermetallic regions.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled high-temperature oxidation/aging treatment (e.g., heating in air at 600–800 °C with a defined dwell time) to stimulate diffusional segregation and phase transformation.
generation.conditions: Tested on alloys with density below 6 g/cm³; experiments to be performed in an oxidizing environment (air) under controlled heating rates and dwell times, comparing as-cast (non-treated) specimens with thermally aged ones.
generation.structural_mediator: Diffusion-driven segregation of Mg leads to the formation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries and interfaces, which serve as preferential sites for MgO nucleation.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates atomic diffusion in the metastable solid solution, causing Mg to segregate into localized regions that then transform into stable Mg-rich intermetallic phases. These intermetallics, due to their higher affinity for oxygen, oxidize to form a compact and adherent MgO scale. This transformation alters the surface chemical potential and imparts improved oxidation resistance as well as modified local corrosion behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast, homogeneous metastable state, the thermally aged specimens will exhibit a microstructure with clearly segregated Mg-rich intermetallic phases, a thinner and more adherent MgO surface layer, and consequently lower corrosion rates and enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly solidified state in which the HEA exists as a largely uniform metastable solid solution with only initially dispersed intermetallic compounds, without induced segregation or a developed surface oxide scale.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and compositions with significant constituent-property differences that favor intermetallic formation. Its validity is anticipated only within the temperature and time regimes (e.g., 600–800 °C, moderate aging durations) where diffusion is active but complete homogenization or undesirable coarsening does not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The rate and extent of Mg segregation, the kinetics of intermetallic phase formation, and the detailed protective nature of the MgO scale under different oxidizing and corrosive conditions are not fully quantified and may vary with minor compositional changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples: one kept in the as-cast state and one subjected to a controlled high-temperature oxidation aging treatment (e.g., heating in air at 600–800 °C for a specified period). Use microstructural analysis (SEM, TEM, EDS mapping, and XRD) to assess the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds and the development of the MgO scale. Then conduct corrosion tests (e.g., electrochemical measurements or salt spray tests) and measure weight gain during oxidation to compare performance between the states.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (XRD and TEM) for detection of Mg-rich intermetallic phases and quantification of grain-boundary segregation
EDS mapping to confirm Mg enrichment at interfaces
Cross-sectional SEM/TEM to measure oxide layer thickness and assess its adherence
Corrosion rate assessment via electrochemical tests or salt spray exposure
Weight gain measurements during oxidation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged specimens do not show significant Mg segregation and formation of distinct Mg-rich intermetallic phases, or if the resulting oxide scale does not exhibit improved adherence and reduced thickness (or no measurable reduction in corrosion rate) compared with the as-cast state, then the hypothesis is rejected.
